Chem. Chem. Phys. 15, 15371, DOI 10.1039/c3cp50968k) in HITRAN2024's file (its sets of reference 32), at their coldest temperature, 203 K, where the liquid is at 90.19 K, linear in wavenumber between the sets' points 1 cm⁻¹ apart, and N = ρ_m N_A = 2.14765 × 10²² cm⁻³ the liquid's number density, so N² = 4.6124 × 10⁴⁴ cm⁻⁶ and a pair's absorption scales with the square of the density: σ 1.19178 × 10⁻⁴⁵ cm⁵ at 575 nm, a = 55.0 m⁻¹ and k = 2.51526 × 10⁻⁶; σ 8.64297 × 10⁻⁴⁶ cm⁵ at 630 nm, a = 39.9 m⁻¹ and k = 1.99858 × 10⁻⁶, to six significant figures. The sets reach 336–654.0 nm, so k = 0 from 655 nm (the B band near 688 nm and the A band near 762 nm are other measurements' and are not drawn), and k = 0 at 390, 395, 400, 405, 410, 415, 420, 425, 430, 455, 595, 600, 650 nm, where the set's σ lies at or below 0 between the bands, within 7 × 10⁻⁴⁸ cm⁵ of it. The bands narrow and their peaks rise on cooling (at 577 nm, 1.11 × 10⁻⁴⁵ cm⁵ at 293 K and 1.36 × 10⁻⁴⁵ cm⁵ at 203 K in the same sets); the 203 K values are not extrapolated to 90 K. k is an extrapolation of the gas's pair absorption, measured near 1 atm, to the liquid, 594 times its number density at 203 K and 1 atm (computed): the liquid's pair correlation at contact, the condensed phase's local-field factor ((n² + 2) ÷ 3)² ÷ n, 1.11 at 575 nm (computed, not applied), and the liquid's band shape are not modelled, so k carries an unmeasured uncertainty. Liveing and Dewar 1892 found the bands "all of exceptional strength" through about 3 inches of the liquid (p. 206), and Liveing and Dewar 1895 "very much more strongly developed by 0.4 centim. of liquid oxygen than by five times that thickness of liquid air" (p. 271), as the file's k has them: at 575 nm it transmits 1.5% through 3 inches and 80% through 0.4 cm (computed). Liquid O2 is blue (Liveing and Dewar 1892, p. 207).
